REMARKS
Claims 21-50 were previously pending. Claims 21, 22, 31-34, 36, and 40-50 have been amended. Claims 1-20 were previously canceled without prejudice to, or disclaimer of, the underlying subject matter. Support for the claim amendments may be found in the original claims and specification; e.g., at [0009], [0160], and [0187] of the as-filed specification. Support for the amendments to the drawings may be found in the as-filed drawings of Provisional Application No. 62/587,337, filed on November 16, 2017, and Provisional Application No. 62/693,810, filed on July 3, 2018, from which this application claims the benefit of No new matter enters by way of the present amendment. Entry of the amendment and reconsideration of the application based on the following remarks is respectfully requested.
I. Claim Objections
The Examiner objects to claims 32 and 36, alleging the following informalities: a. Claim 32 recites "further comprising the step of" when it should most likely recite "further comprising the steps of:". b. Claim 36 recited "The method of claim 23" when it should most likely recite "The method of claim 32."
Office Action at p. 2. Further, the Examiner asserts that, if claim 36 is not meant to depend from claim 32, "claim 36 would be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) for being indefinite because acceleration is not mentioned in any previous claim that claim 36 depends on." Applicant thanks the Examiner for the suggested amendments. Applicant has amended claims 32 and 36. Applicant submits that the claim amendments overcome the objections and respectfully requests the withdrawal of the claim objections based on informalities.
II. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112
The Examiner rejects claims 32 and 33 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. § 112 (pre- AIA), second paragraph, as allegedly "being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention." Id. at 3. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Specifically, the Examiner indicates that there is insufficient antecedent basis for the limitation "the retrieved delta values" in line 2 of claim 32. Without acquiescing to the rejection, and solely to advance prosecution, Applicant has amended claim 31 to recite "querying the database for the delta value and the second delta value of the at least one body location of the patient in the transfer record and the second data record respectively to form retrieved delta values" and amended the dependency of claim 32. The Examiner also indicates that there is insufficient antecedent basis for the limitation "the group of nutritional information" in line 3 of claim 33. Id. Without acquiescing to the rejection, and solely to advance prosecution, Applicant has amended claim 33 to recite "one or more of a nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, an event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result." Applicant submits that the amendments to claims 32 and 33 obviate the rejections, and respectfully requests the withdrawal of the rejections.
III. Rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103
A. Claims 21-25 and 28
The Examiner rejects claims 21-25 and 28 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 for allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Publication 2002/0143262 to Bardy ("Bardy") in view of U.S.
Publication 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. ("Tonar"), and further in view of U.S. Publication 2011/0191122 to Tavakol et al. ("Kharraz Tavakol"). Id. at 4.
Specifically, regarding claim 21, the Examiner alleges that Bardy provides "a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting, the method comprising the steps of: . . . making a plurality of measurements at a body location on the patient at the second care setting, . . . determining whether the value exceeds a threshold, . . . continuing to administer the current intervention if the value does not exceed the threshold, . . . administering a new intervention of level-N if the value exceeds the threshold, where N has a value greater than K... " Id. at 4-5. The Examiner concedes that Bardy "does not explicitly teach SEM measurements, calculating a delta value, and determining if that delta value exceeds a threshold." Id. at 5. The Examiner then cites Tonar for allegedly providing SEM measurements, calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements, and alleges that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the present application to substitute the SEM values provided by Tonar "for myocardial ischemia measurements and myocardial ischemia threshold values as disclosed by Bardy since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Id. at 6. The Examiner also concedes that Bardy fails to specifically provide "identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting." Id. at 6. The Examiner then cites Kharraz Tavakol and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) identify a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting as taught by Kharraz Tavakol in the method as taught by Bardy and Tonar et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of preventing delays in medical care and preventing patient dissuasion from treatment protocol compliance." Id. at 7. Applicant respectfully disagrees. Without acquiescing, and solely to advance prosecution, Applicant amends claim 21 to further recite a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Applicant submits that the Examiner has not established a prima facie case of obviousness for at least the following reasons.
1. No motivation to combine To establish aprima facie case of obviousness, there must be some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings. See, e.g., MPEP § 2143. There must also be a reasonable expectation of success. See, e.g., MPEP § 2143. The teaching or suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art, and not based on the applicant's disclosure. In re Vaeck, 947 F.2d 488, 20 USPQ.2d 1438 (Fed. Cir. 1991). Although obviousness can be established by combining or modifying the teachings of the prior art, "[t]he mere fact that references can be combined or modified does not render the resultant combination obvious unless the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art." MPEP § 2143.01(III) (emphasis in original). Furthermore, "[t]he proposed modification cannot render the prior art unsatisfactory for it intended purpose." MPEP § 2143.01(V). Applicant submits that the Examiner has not met the basic criteria to establish a prima facie case of obviousness, and has not shown that one of ordinary skill in the art would have found suggestion or motivation in the references themselves, or in the knowledge generally available to one of skill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings.
The primary reference Bardy is directed to a "system and method for providing diagnosis and monitoring of myocardial ischemia for use in automated patient care throughout disease onset, progression, regression, and status quo." Bardy at [0002]. Bardy seeks to detect "trends in regularly collected physiological and chemical data indicative of the onset, progression, regression, or status quo of myocardial ischemia diagnosed and monitored using an automated remote patient care system." Id. at [0008]. However, the Examiner alleges that it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to substitute SEM measurements as provided by Tonar "for myocardial ischemia measurements and myocardial ischemia threshold as disclosed by Bardy since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements." Office Action at p. 6. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Applicant submits that Bardy and Tonar are directed to two different pathologies, such that the proposed modification of Bardy renders Bardy unsatisfactory for its intended purpose. In fact, Bardy provides that "[o]ther benefits include an automated, expert system approach to the cross-referral, consideration, and potential finding or elimination of other diseases and health disorders with similar or related etiological indicators and for those other disorders that may have an impact on myocardial ischemia." Bardy at [0095]. Accordingly, a person of ordinary skill in the art reading Bardy would not have simply substituted SEM values used for detecting pressure ulcers for measurements of myocardial ischemia. Since the Examiner's proposed modification renders Bardy unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, there is no suggestion or motivation to make the proposed modification, and the Examiner has not met the basic criteria to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.
2. Improper use of hindsight It is improper, in determining whether a person of ordinary skill would have been led to this combination of references, simply to "[use] that which the inventor taught against its teacher." In re Lee, 277 F.3d at 1343, citing W.L. Gore & Assocs. v. Garlock, Inc., 721 F.2d 1540, 1553 (Fed. Cir. 1983). See In re Dow Chem. Co., 837 F.2d 469, 473 (Fed. Cir. 1988) ("[t]here must be a reason or suggestion in the art for selecting the procedure used, other than the knowledge learned from the applicant's disclosure"); Cardiac Pacemakers, Inc. v. St. Jude Medical, Inc., 381 F.3d 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2004) ("the suggestion to combine references must not be derived by hindsight from knowledge of the invention itself."). Using an applicant's disclosure as a blueprint to reconstruct the claimed invention from isolated pieces of the prior art contravenes the statutory mandate of § 103 which requires judging obviousness at the point in time when the invention was made. See Grain Processing Corp. v. American Maize-Prods. Co., 840 F.2d 902, 907 (Fed. Cir. 1988).
Here, it appears that the Examiner has applied impermissible hindsight to improperly interpret the claimed subj ect matter. As discussed above, one of ordinary skill in the art would have lacked the motivation to combine at least Bardy with Tonar. Since any motivation to combine the cited references can only have been gleaned in view of the instant specification, Applicant submits that the Examiner appears to be using impermissible hindsight to improperly interpret the claimed subject matter as obvious over Bardy in view of Tonar and Kharraz Tavakol.
For at least the above reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of amended claim 21. "[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, dependent claims 22-25 and 28 should also be allowable due to their dependence from amended claim 21.
B. Claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38 The Examiner rejects claims 26, 29, 30, 37, and 38 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al. ("Ploetz"). Specifically for claim 26, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach that "the record further comprises a date and a time when said first scan was performed." Office Action at 10. The Examiner cites Ploetz for remedying the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol, and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the record further comprises a date and a time when said first scan was performed as taught by Ploetz et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of providing accurate and detailed records of the health status of a patient." Id. at 11. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Ploetz at best provides a "method and a system for monitoring the regular collection of operational data from a multiplicity of remotely located medical imaging systems by a central service facility, and starting a corrective action process if the collection of operational data deviates from a historical norm based on the frequency of reception and the volume of the data received from the data source." Ploetz at col. 3, 11. 11-17. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Ploetz provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Ploetz does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 26. "[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, dependent claims 29, 30, 37, and 38 should also be allowable due to their dependence from amended claim 26.
C. Claim 27
The Examiner rejects claim 27 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 22, and further in view of U.S. Patent 9,028,407 to Bennett-Guerrero ("Bennett-Guerrero"). Specifically, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol "fails to further, specifically teach continuing to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold." Office Action at 16-17. The Examiner cites Bennett-Guerrero for remedying the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol, and alleges that one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention would have found it obvious to "continue to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold as taught by Bennett- Guerrero in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of being beneficial for various reasons such as to enhance, improve or even optimize battery life." Id. at 17. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Bennett-Guerrero at best provides an apparatus for monitoring patient orientation. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Bennett-Guerrero provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Bennett-Guerrero does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 27.
D. Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39
The Examiner rejects claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol, and further in view of Ploetz as applied to claim 30, and further in view of U.S. Patent 9,675,289 to Heaton ("Heaton"). Specifically for claim 31, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, and Ploetz fails to teach the step of "querying the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values." Id. at 18. Similarly for claim 39, the Examiner alleges that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, and Ploetz teaches the method of claim 37, but concedes that the combination fails to teach the step of "querying the database to retrieve the values observed over time for a particular patient across multiple care settings and various episodes of care." Id. at 20. The Examiner cites Heaton for allegedly providing the step of "querying the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values," and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to query the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values as taught be Heaton in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to view and analyze stored data in a chronological form so that trends in data may be observed." Id. at 18-19. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Heaton at best provides "a method for monitoring individual metabolic response and for generating nutritional feedback." The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Heaton provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Heaton does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, and Ploetz. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of amended claims 31 and 39. "[I]f an independent claim is nonobvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, then any claim depending therefrom is nonobvious." In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071 (Fed. Cir. 1988). Thus, dependent claims 32 and 34 should also be allowable due to their dependence from amended claim 31.
E. Claim 331
The Examiner rejects claim 33 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol, and further in view of Ploetz as applied to claim 30, and further in view of U.S. Publication 2008/0015894 to Miller et al. ("Miller"). Specifically for claim 33, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, and Ploetz fails to teach the steps of creating an additional data record and reporting the additional data record to the database. The Examiner cites Miller for allegedly providing the steps of "creating an additional data record that comprises the patient identifier, a data element from the group of nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, lean event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result, and a date/time associated with the data element. . . and reporting the additional data record to the database," and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was 1 Per the Office Action, Claims 31, 32, 34, and 39 are rejected; however, Applicant understands that claim 33 is rejected here instead.
filed would have found it obvious to have the steps. . . as taught by Miller et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of monitoring all relevant patient information that affect a patient's health status so that appropriate recommendations may be made." Id. at 22. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Miller at best provides methods of assessing a health risk associated with a medication therapy regimen and intervention thereof. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Miller provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Miller does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, and Ploetz. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of amended claim 33.
F. Claim 35
The Examiner rejects claim 35 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, Ploetz, Heaton, and further in view of U.S. Patent No.
8,355,925 to Rothman et al. ("Rothman"). Specifically for claim 35, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, Ploetz, and Heaton fails to teach the step of analyzing the retrieved delta values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value. The Examiner cites Rothman for allegedly providing this step, and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the steps... as taught by Rothman et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., Ploetz et al., and Heaton in combination with the motivation(s) of alerting a user if a patient is getting better or worse at an accelerating rate." Id. at 23-24. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Rothman at best provides methods of assessing risk based on medical data. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Rothman provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Rothman does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, Kharraz Tavakol, Ploetz, and Heaton. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of amended claim 35.
G. Claim 36
The Examiner rejects claim 36 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar and Kharraz Tavakol, and further in view of Rothman. Specifically for claim 36, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach that the acceleration is determined by the rate of change of the slope of the curve. The Examiner cites Rothman for allegedly providing this, and alleges that "[o]ne of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have wherein acceleration is determined by the rate of change of the slope of the curve as taught by Rothman et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of alerting a user if a patient is getting better or worse at an accelerating rate." Id. at 23-24. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Rothman at best provides methods of assessing risk based on medical data. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Rothman provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Rothman does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 36.
H. Claims 40 and 43
The Examiner rejects claims 40 and 43 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar and Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Protocol for the successful treatment of pressure ulcers" to Brem et al. (The American Journal of Surgery, 188 (Suppl to July 2004): 9S-17S (2004)) ("Brem"). Specifically for claim 40, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-0 intervention selected from a group consisting of providing good nutrition, standard mattress, turning every 24 hours, and a combination thereof." Id. at 25. Similarly for claim 43, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-3 intervention of applying dressing to the back or sides of patient's heel." Id. at 26. The Examiner cites Brem for allegedly providing these interventions, and alleges that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-0 intervention. . . as taught by Brem et al. for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of elements." Id. at 25-26. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Brem at best provides protocols for the successful treatment of pressure ulcers. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Brem provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Brem does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 40 and 43.
. Claim 41
The Examiner rejects claim 41 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent 5,367,789 to Lamont ("Lamont"). Specifically for claim 41, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-1 intervention of providing a heel boot to the patient." Id. at 27. The Examiner cites Lamont for allegedly providing this intervention, and alleges that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-1 intervention. . . as taught by Lamont for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of elements." Id. at 27. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Lamont at best provides a soft medical boot having an articulated splint bar for adjusting the angle of the foot of a patient disposed in a supine position. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Lamont provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Lamont does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 41.
J. Claim 42
The Examiner rejects claim 42 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent 6,634,045 to DuDonis et al. ("DuDonis"). Specifically for claim 42, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-2 intervention of changing the patient's support surface." Id. at 28. The Examiner cites Lamont for allegedly providing this intervention, and alleges that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-2 intervention... as taught by DuDonis et al. for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of elements." Id. at 28. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
DuDonis at best provides a heel elevating foam cushion used to relieve heel pressure ulcers in patients confined to bed. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that DuDonis provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, DuDonis does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 42.
K. Claim 44
The Examiner rejects claim 44 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Friction between human skin and medical textiles for decubitus prevention" to Rotaru et al.
(Tribology International, 65:91-96 (2013)) ("Rotaru"). Specifically for claim 44, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-4 intervention of changing the patient's sheet cover to a low-friction sheet cover." Id. at 29. The Examiner cites Rotaru for allegedly providing this intervention, and alleges that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-2 intervention. . . as taught by Rotaru et al. for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of elements." Id. at 29. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Rotaru at best provides that the risk of pressure ulcers could be reduced by improved hospital bed sheets. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Rotaru provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Rotaru does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 44. L. Claim 45
The Examiner rejects claim 45 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,011,041 to Hann ("Hann"). Specifically for claim 45, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-5 intervention of providing a low-friction padded mattress surface for the patient's lower leg." Id. at 30. The Examiner cites Hann for allegedly providing this intervention, and alleges that "it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute a level-5 intervention. . . as taught by Hann for a treatment program of a certain diagnostic level as disclosed by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of elements." Id. at 30-31. Applicant respectfully disagrees.
Hann at best provides a multilayer support surface, such as an underpad, for preventing pressure sores in a patient. The Examiner does not otherwise allege that Hann provides any suggestion or motivation to combine the references, much less modify the teachings to arrive at the claimed subject matter, that of a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient having or at risk of developing pressure ulcers during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting. Accordingly, Hann does not remedy the deficiencies of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol. Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claim 45.
M. Claims 46 and 47
The Examiner rejects claims 46 and 47 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Bardy in view of Tonar, further in view of Kharraz Tavakol as applied to claim 21, and further in view of "Prevention and treatment of pressure ulcers" to Thomas (J. Am. Med. Dir. Assoc., 7:46- 59 (2006)) ("Thomas"). Specifically for claim 46, the Examiner concedes that the combination of Bardy, Tonar, and Kharraz Tavakol fails to teach "a level-6 intervention of turning the patient at a shorter interval than currently provided for." Id. at 31.
